title: Baseline retest for cores/bench
Collapse forwarding into one-hot operand selects
motivation:
The current worst path starts at the MEM/WB destination register and crosses
forwarding control, the EX operand mux, and the ALU before reaching memory-side
outputs. The encoded forwarding select followed by a second operand mux adds
serial selection logic on this path.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Generate mutually exclusive direct-source enables for the register value,
EX/MEM result, and MEM/WB result, preserving EX/MEM priority and x0 behavior.
Use those enables in a parallel masked-OR operand mux in EX. This should remove
the encoded-select decode stage and shorten the high-fanout forwarding path
without changing pipeline timing or architectural behavior.

title: Move division into an iterative unit
motivation: The measured critical path passes through the EX forwarding and ALU cone and is about 200 ns. The current ALU describes signed and unsigned quotient and remainder as combinational division operators, which can create a very deep datapath even though CoreMark rarely needs division.

hypothesis.motivation: The measured critical path passes through the EX forwarding and ALU cone and is about 200 ns. The current ALU describes signed and unsigned quotient and remainder as combinational division operators, which can create a very deep datapath even though CoreMark rarely needs division.
hypothesis.hypothesis: Replace the combinational DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU datapath with a shared iterative divider that runs only for M-extension divide and remainder instructions. Hold younger pipeline work while it iterates, then retire the result in order; leave ordinary ALU and multiply operations single-cycle. This should remove the divider from the normal EX critical path and reduce LUT use, with cycle cost limited to divide instructions. Preserve divide-by-zero and signed-overflow results, and keep the RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS behavior on its existing tractable bypass path.

title: Add a small dynamic branch predictor
motivation:
The current core resolves conditional branches and jumps in EX, then redirects
fetch and flushes the following instruction. CoreMark has repeated loop
branches, so avoiding that recovery bubble on correctly predicted control
flow can improve iterations per cycle without changing the ISA or retirement
contract.

hypothesis.motivation:
The current core resolves conditional branches and jumps in EX, then redirects
fetch and flushes the following instruction. CoreMark has repeated loop
branches, so avoiding that recovery bubble on correctly predicted control
flow can improve iterations per cycle without changing the ISA or retirement
contract.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a 16-entry, PC-indexed two-bit saturating direction table, initialized to
weakly not-taken and trained once when a valid conditional branch resolves in
EX. Predict direct JAL instructions taken, derive branch/JAL targets from the
fetched instruction, and carry each instruction's predicted next PC through
ID/EX. EX should redirect and flush only when the resolved next PC differs
from that prediction. Gate speculative PC advancement on fetch being
unstalled, and suppress repeated predictor training while EX is held by a
data-memory stall. This should remove the taken-branch bubble on correctly
predicted CoreMark loops with little predictor state and no target-table
lookup.

title: Decode register file reads in parallel
motivation:
After removing combinational division, the critical path now runs from a
register-file bit through the ID read path into the ID/EX operand register.
The current variable-indexed array read can map as a deep 32-to-1 mux for
each of the two source ports.

hypothesis.hypothesis:

title: Retiming branch squash out of the redirect path
motivation: After making DIV/REM iterative, the measured worst path runs from the register file through ID and EX, then through IF and hazard control back into ID. A resolved branch currently fans out through same-cycle fetch flushing and ID-stage flushing, extending the EX-to-PC redirect path with squash control.

hypothesis.motivation: After making DIV/REM iterative, the measured worst path runs from the register file through ID and EX, then through IF and hazard control back into ID. A resolved branch currently fans out through same-cycle fetch flushing and ID-stage flushing, extending the EX-to-PC redirect path with squash control.
hypothesis.hypothesis: Keep branch resolution and the PC redirect in EX, but replace same-cycle redirect fanout into the IF payload and hazard-driven ID flush with a registered squash token in ID. When a redirect advances and a valid younger fetch is present, let that instruction enter ID/EX and mask its output to a bubble for the following cycle; the target instruction then enters normally. Track redirects already applied while ID is held, so releasing a data-memory stall does not mistakenly squash the target fetch. Do not create a squash token when the fetch is invalid due to an instruction-memory stall. This retimes wrong-path invalidation across a register boundary and should shorten the measured redirect-to-ID control path without adding an IF target adder or predictor lookup.

motivation: The prior branch predictor regressed because it decoded fetched branch immediates and added them to the PC in the fetch-to-PC path. That path is timing sensitive. title: Keep ID payload out of flush control
motivation: After the iterative divider improved timing, the worst path crosses EX branch resolution, IF redirect, hazard control, and returns to the ID/EX register. A redirect currently clears the entire ID/EX bundle, placing that long control path on every payload bit's input mux.

title: Register branch redirect feedback
motivation:
The current critical path runs from register-file operands through EX branch
resolution, then back through fetch and hazard control into ID. EX redirect
fanout makes a register-dependent branch decision affect multiple pipeline
controls in the same cycle, keeping this cross-stage feedback path long.

hypothesis.motivation:

resolution, then back through fetch and hazard control into ID. EX redirect
fanout makes a register-dependent branch decision affect multiple pipeline
controls in the same cycle, keeping this cross-stage feedback path long.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a one-entry registered redirect handoff between EX resolution and fetch.
Capture the resolved target only when its instruction advances, squash the
younger instruction immediately, and apply the target from the pending
register on the following cycle while suppressing stale fetch data. Keep a
pending redirect until the PC update is applied, and prevent a held EX
instruction from enqueueing the same redirect repeatedly. This adds a
recovery cycle for taken control flow, but removes branch comparison and
EX-to-fetch/hazard fanout from the same-cycle path into ID; the shorter
register-to-register path may raise Fmax enough to offset the small CoreMark
IPC cost.

title: Pipeline sequential-lookahead BTB reads
motivation:
CoreMark repeats loop control flow, but prior predictors put target lookup or
target generation directly on the fetch-to-PC path and reduced Fmax. The core
can look up the next sequential PC one cycle ahead, register the result, and
keep predictor table access off the PC selection path during ordinary fetch.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a small tagged BTB with direction counters and perform its lookup for
PC+4 during the preceding cycle. Register the hit, direction, tag, and target
so that when the matching PC becomes current, fetch selects the registered
prediction without a combinational table lookup. Carry the predicted next PC
with the instruction and have EX recover only when the architecturally
resolved next PC differs. Invalidate lookahead metadata on redirects, hold it
across fetch stalls, and train once for each advancing valid control-flow
instruction. The registered lookup should preserve loop prediction benefits
while removing tag comparison and target selection from the fetch-to-PC path.

title: Bypass general ALU selection for memory addresses
motivation: The champion's worst path launches from the register file and reaches the memory-side address through ID and EX. Loads and stores always calculate an address as rs1 plus the decoded immediate, but currently pass through general ALU operand muxes and ALU operation selection.

hypothesis.motivation: The champion's worst path launches from the register file and reaches the memory-side address through ID and EX. Loads and stores always calculate an address as rs1 plus the decoded immediate, but currently pass through general ALU operand muxes and ALU operation selection.
hypothesis.hypothesis: Add a dedicated effective-address sum in EX using the forwarded rs1 and instruction immediate, and route that sum to EX/MEM for loads and stores. This removes the general ALU's operand and result selection from the address path while leaving branch, jump, arithmetic, divider, store-data forwarding, and retirement behavior unchanged. The extra adder may cost some LUTs, but the direct address path should shorten the current critical path and improve Fmax.

title: Decouple fetch with a small instruction queue
motivation: The pipeline currently couples instruction fetch directly to decode: an instruction-memory stall injects a bubble, while a data-memory stall freezes fetch entirely. The independent random stalls can therefore waste cycles even when fetch could have prefetched during a backend hold. A small queue can preserve fetched instructions across those stalls and reduce front-end bubbles without changing retirement order.

hypothesis.motivation: The pipeline currently couples instruction fetch directly to decode: an instruction-memory stall injects a bubble, while a data-memory stall freezes fetch entirely. The independent random stalls can therefore waste cycles even when fetch could have prefetched during a backend hold. A small queue can preserve fetched instructions across those stalls and reduce front-end bubbles without changing retirement order.
hypothesis.hypothesis: Add a two-entry instruction queue between fetch and decode, with a separate fetch PC that advances only when an instruction is accepted. Let fetch continue filling the queue while decode is held by a data-memory or divide stall, and let decode consume queued instructions during short instruction-memory stalls. Flush queued entries on a resolved redirect and restart fetching at its target; hold the front entry through load-use and backend stalls. Keep existing instruction validity and RVFI retirement semantics. The queue should reduce cycles lost to the interaction between the two random bus stalls, while keeping the fetch address path independent of queue contents.

title: Predict function returns with a small return stack
motivation:
The earlier direction-table and BTB predictors regressed after adding
decode, lookup, and target selection logic to the fetch path. CoreMark
repeatedly calls and returns from helper functions, and ABI-style returns
have a target already recorded when their calls execute. A small register
stack can supply that target without a tagged target-table lookup.

hypothesis.motivation:
The earlier direction-table and BTB predictors regressed after adding

repeatedly calls and returns from helper functions, and ABI-style returns
have a target already recorded when their calls execute. A small register
stack can supply that target without a tagged target-table lookup.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a shallow shift-register return-address stack. Push PC+4 when an
advancing JAL/JALR writes x1 or x5, and predict a fetched JALR with rd=x0,
rs1=x1 or x5, and imm=0 to the current stack top. Carry the predicted next
PC with the instruction; EX compares it with the resolved next PC, pops
the stack for a valid advancing return, and redirects only on a mismatch.
Keep conditional branches and other jumps on the existing sequential
prediction path. This targets frequent function-return recovery bubbles
with a small, direct register-to-PC mux and avoids a BTB tag comparison or
branch-target adder in fetch.

title: Share the RV32M multiplier datapath
motivation:
The current champion's worst path crosses the EX ALU, and alu.sv describes
separate full-width signed-signed, unsigned-unsigned, and signed-unsigned
products. These parallel multipliers consume FPGA arithmetic resources and
add routing around an already timing-sensitive execution cone.

hypothesis.motivation:
The current champion's worst path crosses the EX ALU, and alu.sv describes
separate full-width signed-signed, unsigned-unsigned, and signed-unsigned
products. These parallel multipliers consume FPGA arithmetic resources and
add routing around an already timing-sensitive execution cone.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the three parallel product expressions with one 33-by-33 signed
product. Select each operand's extension bit from the operation: sign-extend
both for MULH, sign-extend only rs1 for MULHSU, and zero-extend both for
MULHU and MUL. The low 32 product bits remain correct for MUL, while bits
63:32 provide the corresponding high-half result. Sharing the product
should reduce DSP and routing pressure in EX, giving place and route more
room to improve Fmax without changing instruction latency. Keep the
RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS substitutions intact and validate all four real
arithmetic results against the existing ALU vectors and cosim.

motivation:
The RV32IM ALU currently describes separate signed-signed, unsigned-unsigned,
and signed-unsigned 64-bit products, although only one multiply result is
selected for an instruction. The current timed path passes through EX and
the ALU, and the FPGA build uses six DSP blocks. Sharing the product unit
could reduce arithmetic duplication and placement pressure on the datapath.

title: Tiny taken-target cache with deferred recovery
motivation:
CoreMark repeatedly executes loop branches, while the current EX branch
resolution feeds back through fetch and hazard control into ID. Earlier
predictors hurt timing by adding fetched-instruction decode, a larger tagged
lookup, or return-stack selection to the PC path.

hypothesis.motivation:
CoreMark repeatedly executes loop branches, while the current EX branch
resolution feeds back through fetch and hazard control into ID. Earlier
predictors hurt timing by adding fetched-instruction decode, a larger tagged
lookup, or return-stack selection to the PC path.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a two-entry fully tagged taken-target cache trained by valid, advancing
taken conditional branches in EX. A fetch hit predicts the cached target;
a miss predicts PC+4. Carry the predicted next PC with the instruction and
compare it with the resolved next PC in EX. On a mismatch, squash the
younger instruction and capture the actual target in a recovery register;
apply that registered target on the following cycle instead of feeding EX
resolution through same-cycle PC and hazard feedback. Qualify training and
recovery against pipeline holds so stalls cannot duplicate updates. This
keeps instruction decode and target addition out of fetch, gives recurring
taken loops a one-cycle prediction, and confines the long recovery path to
occasional misses.

title: Share branch comparison logic
motivation: The current critical path runs from the register file through EX branch resolution and the redirect and hazard feedback into ID. Branch resolution selects among separate equality, signed comparison, and unsigned comparison expressions, with paired less-than and greater-or-equal operations that are logical complements.

hypothesis.motivation: The current critical path runs from the register file through EX branch resolution and the redirect and hazard feedback into ID. Branch resolution selects among separate equality, signed comparison, and unsigned comparison expressions, with paired less-than and greater-or-equal operations that are logical complements.
hypothesis.hypothesis: Factor EX branch evaluation into one equality result and one unsigned less-than result. Derive signed less-than from the operand sign bits and the unsigned result, then implement BEQ/BNE, BLT/BGE, and BLTU/BGEU as each result or its complement. This should reduce duplicate compare logic and shorten the EX-to-redirect feedback path while preserving all branch outcomes and pipeline timing.

title: Retiming register-file reads into synchronous memory banks
motivation:
Timing reports repeatedly show paths beginning at the register-file array and
crossing execute or branch control before reaching fetch and decode state.
The current asynchronous 32-entry, two-read mux is both a large LUT structure
and the source of operands on these long paths.

hypothesis.motivation:
Timing reports repeatedly show paths beginning at the register-file array and
crossing execute or branch control before reaching fetch and decode state.
The current asynchronous 32-entry, two-read mux is both a large LUT structure
and the source of operands on these long paths.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the resettable asynchronous register array with two identical
write-through memory copies, each with one synchronous read port, so the
FPGA can map the register file reads into embedded RAM. Register the read
address and same-cycle write-bypass metadata alongside the decoded
instruction in ID, keeping operands aligned with the existing ID/EX boundary
and sustaining one instruction per cycle. Use resettable per-register
initialization-valid bits to preserve the current zero-after-reset behavior
without resetting the RAM contents, and retain x0 and WB bypass semantics.
Removing the distributed 32-to-1 read mux from the execute/redirect timing
cone should improve Fmax and free LUTs while adding no read-latency stage.

title: Register lookahead branch target predictions
motivation: The last small taken-target cache reduced branch misses but still put its tag lookup and target selection on the fetch-to-PC path. Earlier predictor attempts show that this path is timing-sensitive, while recurring CoreMark loop branches can repay a small prediction table through fewer redirect bubbles.

hypothesis.motivation: The last small taken-target cache reduced branch misses but still put its tag lookup and target selection on the fetch-to-PC path. Earlier predictor attempts show that this path is timing-sensitive, while recurring CoreMark loop branches can repay a small prediction table through fewer redirect bubbles.
hypothesis.hypothesis: Keep a two-entry fully tagged cache of taken conditional-branch targets, but look up the next PC and register the hit and target alongside the PC update. Fetch then selects a predicted target using registered metadata, keeping the tag comparison out of the current PC feedback path. Carry the predicted next PC with each instruction, and have EX redirect only when its resolved next PC differs. Train or invalidate the cache only once when a valid branch advances, so bus holds cannot repeat updates. This should preserve loop prediction benefits while protecting Fmax from the combinational BTB lookup.

title: Retiming forwarding selection into ID/EX
motivation:
The current critical path starts at a destination register in EX/MEM and
passes through forwarding comparison and selection, the EX operand mux, and
the ALU before reaching the memory address output. The register-file read
path has already been shortened, leaving forwarding control on this path.

hypothesis.motivation:
The current critical path starts at a destination register in EX/MEM and
passes through forwarding comparison and selection, the EX operand mux, and
the ALU before reaching the memory address output. The register-file read
path has already been shortened, leaving forwarding control on this path.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Compute each incoming instruction's forwarding source while it is accepted
into ID/EX, by comparing its source registers with the current ID/EX and
EX/MEM destinations. Store the two small source selectors alongside the
instruction and use them in EX with the existing live EX/MEM and MEM/WB data
buses. Give the younger ID/EX producer priority, exclude x0 and nonwriters,
and account for a load-use bubble so a load is selected from MEM/WB only once
its data is available. Holding selectors with ID/EX across stalls and
flushing them with bubbles should preserve alignment while removing tag
compares and priority logic from the EX forwarding-to-ALU path.

title: Split operand forwarding from execute
motivation:
The latest timing report has its critical path running from the forwarding
network through the EX ALU to a memory-side output. The synchronous register
file already removed the earlier read-mux bottleneck, so the remaining serial
forwarding and execution work is a good candidate for a pipeline boundary.

hypothesis.motivation:
The latest timing report has its critical path running from the forwarding
network through the EX ALU to a memory-side output. The synchronous register
file already removed the earlier read-mux bottleneck, so the remaining serial
forwarding and execution work is a good candidate for a pipeline boundary.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Divide EX into an operand stage and an execute stage. Resolve source operands
and forwarding in the first stage, then register operands, immediate, control,
and instruction metadata before the ALU, branch comparison, and effective
address logic in the second stage. Preserve one-instruction-per-cycle flow
with forwarding from the later stages, and update stall, flush, divider, and
retirement control for the extra boundary. The added register should separate
forwarding selection from the ALU path and raise Fmax; the cost is a longer
taken-branch recovery path and more pipeline state.

title: Validate registered BTB predictions in MEM
motivation:
Repeated CoreMark loop branches can avoid taken-branch recovery when a
cached target is predicted correctly. Earlier predictors hurt timing by
putting BTB lookup on the PC update path or by feeding a full-width
predicted-versus-resolved PC comparison from EX back into fetch.

hypothesis.motivation:
Repeated CoreMark loop branches can avoid taken-branch recovery when a
cached target is predicted correctly. Earlier predictors hurt timing by
putting BTB lookup on the PC update path or by feeding a full-width
predicted-versus-resolved PC comparison from EX back into fetch.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a small tagged branch target buffer with two-bit direction counters,
and register its lookup metadata in step with each fetch PC so target-table
selection is not part of the current PC feedback path. Carry the predicted
next PC with the instruction, but validate it against the resolved next PC
after EX, in MEM. A mismatch then squashes speculative younger instructions
and redirects fetch from the MEM-stage state; train the table once per
resolved control-flow instruction, including across memory stalls. Correct
loop predictions remove taken-branch bubbles, while moving prediction
correction out of the RF-to-EX-to-fetch path should protect Fmax.

title: Segment the EX arithmetic carry path
motivation:
The current champion's worst path runs from the registered EX operand through
the ALU to the memory address output. Load and store effective addresses use
a 32-bit addition, so carry propagation in that arithmetic cone can limit
clock frequency for a large fraction of CoreMark instructions.

hypothesis.motivation:
The current champion's worst path runs from the registered EX operand through
the ALU to the memory address output. Load and store effective addresses use
a 32-bit addition, so carry propagation in that arithmetic cone can limit
clock frequency for a large fraction of CoreMark instructions.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the ALU's plain 32-bit ADD expression with a four-block adder that
computes 8-bit block generate and propagate terms and resolves block carries
in parallel. Keep the existing ALU interface, result selection, and other
operations unchanged. Limiting local carry propagation to each 8-bit block
should shorten the effective-address path while preserving exact RV32I
addition results and one-cycle execution.

title: Pipeline the critical arithmetic path
motivation:
The best current design has already separated operand forwarding from EX,
and its measured critical path now runs from the registered operands through
the EX ALU to the memory-side address path. Branch prediction and fetch
buffering have regressed on this core, so shortening the remaining arithmetic
stage is the strongest structural opportunity.

hypothesis.motivation:
The best current design has already separated operand forwarding from EX,
and its measured critical path now runs from the registered operands through
the EX ALU to the memory-side address path. Branch prediction and fetch
buffering have regressed on this core, so shortening the remaining arithmetic
stage is the strongest structural opportunity.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Split execute into two pipelined stages and implement the common 32-bit
add/subtract and comparison work as 16-bit segments. The first stage should
compute the low-half carry and both possible high-half results in parallel;
the second should select the correct upper result and resolve branches.
Pass other single-cycle ALU results through the same two-stage boundary so
independent instructions can still flow at one per cycle. Retiming forwarding,
redirects, memory requests, and divide completion with the new boundary should
reduce the longest arithmetic delay without serializing ordinary instructions;
the main cost is a deeper branch-recovery path and extra hazard bookkeeping.

title: Early backward-taken branch prediction
motivation:
The current core resolves conditional branches in EX, so taken branches
redirect fetch only after younger work has entered the pipeline. CoreMark
has recurring backward loop branches, while prior BTB designs added costly
lookup and prediction-validation paths to fetch timing.

hypothesis.motivation:
The current core resolves conditional branches in EX, so taken branches
redirect fetch only after younger work has entered the pipeline. CoreMark
has recurring backward loop branches, while prior BTB designs added costly
lookup and prediction-validation paths to fetch timing.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Use a static backward-taken, forward-not-taken predictor for conditional
branches, and predict direct JAL instructions taken. Decode and register the
branch target with the instruction before applying the prediction, keeping
instruction decode and target generation out of the fetch-PC feedback path.
When a registered branch reaches the prediction point, redirect fetch early
for predicted-taken control flow and squash the younger sequential fetch.
Carry the predicted direction through the pipeline and let EX redirect only
on a direction mismatch; leave JALR prediction to the existing EX resolution.
This should remove the EX recovery bubble on correctly predicted loop
branches without a BTB, tag comparison, or fetch-stage target adder.
